title: Point Slider
context: Grade 4, and this is the step where a printed rule and its own worked example disagree with each other. The rule as printed sends the filling zeros to the wrong side of the numerator. The worked example directly beneath it puts them on the left and says so three separate times. Zeros hung past the right hand end of a nine build nine hundred, and the point counted in from there lands on nine whole ones where nine hundredths was wanted, which is a hundred times too big and looks perfectly tidy written down. Every answer printed in this chapter is arithmetically right, so nothing that checks the sums would ever find this.

writeup.why: Turn a fraction into a decimal by counting the zeros underneath, and find out which side the filling zeros go on when the digits run out.
writeup.look: A fraction at the top with its denominator lit, the numerator laid out in digit cards below it, and a second lane under that running the other way.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Point Slider' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the fractions turned against the fractions this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each decimal is read back and the second fixed at however many this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The fraction stands at the top left of the working area, 300 by 140 at 64,206, its bar drawn near-black, its numerator above and its denominator below with the denominator lit. The zero counter sits beside it, 260 by 76 at 400,230: it counts the zeros of the denominator one at a time, lighting each zero in the denominator as it is counted, and writes the number of decimal places it has found, which is the only number it ever shows. The digit cards lie in a row across the middle of the working area at 300,370, each 96 by 116, one digit to a card, laid out from the numerator with no gaps between them. The point card is a narrower card 56 by 116 in vermilion and it waits just past their right hand end; it slides leftwards one whole digit at a time, the counter tracking each step, and it cannot be dropped until it has moved as many digits as the counter is holding. Where the digits run out before the count is met, the places still empty are drawn as outlined card spaces and lit BETWEEN the point card and the digits already there, that is on the LEFT of those digits, and a short arrow is drawn running inward from the point to the nearest empty one. The zero tray stands under the row at 300,500, offering grey zeros; a zero dropped into a lit empty place settles at the same size and weight as every other card, and a zero dropped past the right hand end of the digits is refused and springs back with nothing marked, the empty places on the left lit again and the arrow redrawn running inward from the point. The wrong side lane runs at 64,530, 1080 by 120: it loads the same fraction, hangs the zeros past the right hand end instead, walks its own point card in from the right of what that built, and carries the working all the way to a finished answer. The distance bar is drawn at 64,662, 1080 by 60, between the two answers, with how many times apart they are written along it. Neither lane is marked, neither is cleared, and the bar measures rather than judges. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever an answer is asked for, with a point key beside them and, under those, a zero key drawn grey that can only be pressed while a place on the left is lit and waiting, so that the pad and the tray agree about which side a filling zero goes on. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a digit standing to the left of the point is deep blue, a digit standing to the right of it is green, and the point itself is vermilion between them on every phase without exception. A part or a column standing for tenths is amber, one standing for hundredths is rose, one standing for thousandths is sky blue, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey, whether it was written in on the left of a short numerator or printed on the end of a measurement. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every one of the readings survives with the colour taken away, because a place is told by the heading written over it before it is ever told by a colour, a filling zero is told by the short arrow running inward from the point, and a zero printed on the end is told by the place counter that lights it. Grey never means faint: such a zero is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. The arrow that marks a filling zero always runs inward, from the point towards the digits, and it is never drawn running the other way on any phase of this tool, including inside the wrong side lane, where the zeros are hung past the right hand end with no arrow drawn at all. The direction of that arrow is the whole of the teaching and it is never used for decoration.
writeup.finish: The card shows the fraction the child converted, its decimal with the places counted from the point, and any zeros they filled standing in front of the digits.

phases.win: the counter settles and that many empty places are drawn to the right of a point
phases.does: counts the zeros underneath and sets the counter to that many places
phases.goal: the zeros in the denominator count the decimal places
phases.says: Count the zeros underneath. That is how many places you need.
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many decimal places does a bottom number of a thousand ask for, and how do you know?
phases.feels: the bottom number is doing the deciding, and only its zeros are being counted
phases.hands: Write three fractions on the board with ten, a hundred and a thousand underneath them, and have the class count the zeros aloud and write only that count down, with nothing else attempted yet. Then draw that many empty boxes to the right of a point for each one. Ask what would change if the bottom number were ten thousand, and let them answer by counting rather than by rule.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of the two numbers is the bottom one? Second rung, the phase's: how many zeros has it got? Third rung: the fraction is cut to a denominator of ten and the child counts it and draws the places. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a hundred plainly has three digits and the count of digits is the easier thing to see, and for a denominator of ten the two counts are only one apart.
wrong.move: counts the digits of the denominator instead of its zeros, so a hundred asks for three decimal places.
wrong.screen: the counter runs again slowly with each zero of the denominator lighting as it is counted and the leading one left plain and uncounted, and the number it finds is written beside the child's count rather than over it. That many empty places are then drawn to the right of a point, and the child's count is drawn as a second row of places underneath, one longer.

wrong.why: the numerator is where the cards are laid out and where everything else is about to happen, so it is where the eye already is.
wrong.move: counts the zeros of the numerator, or its digits, because the top number is the one being worked on.
wrong.screen: the denominator lights on its own with the bar drawn heavier between the two, and the counter is walked across from the top number to the bottom one along a drawn path before it counts. The child's count stays written beside the counter, the numerator is dimmed to nothing but its outline while the counting runs, and both numbers stay on the stage afterwards.

phases.screen: a fraction at the top with its denominator lit and the counter still empty
phases.soWhat: The zeros in the denominator count the decimal places, one place for each zero.

phases.win: the point drops on the counted digit and the decimal is read back from the point outwards
phases.does: slides the point card leftwards one digit at a time until the count is met
phases.goal: the point goes in from the right hand end of the numerator
phases.says: Start at the right hand end and walk the point in. Count as you go.
phases.check: Turn a three digit numerator over a thousand into a decimal, and say which end you started counting from.
phases.feels: the walk starts at the right hand end every time, and the counting is what stops it
phases.hands: Give each group a fraction card and the loose digits of its numerator, laid out in a row on the desk with a card marked with a point beside them. They count the zeros below, then slide the point card in from the right hand end, one digit at a time, counting out loud as it goes. Then ask what they would have got by starting from the other end, and let one group try it and read the answer out.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many places does the counter say? Second rung, the phase's: which end does the point card start from? Third rung: the row is cut to two digit cards and the child walks the point in on them. The number pad and the point key stay open.

wrong.why: reading and counting both start at the left in everything else, and the left hand end of the row is where a hand naturally lands.
wrong.move: counts the point in from the LEFT hand end of the numerator, so a three digit numerator over a thousand comes out ten times too big.
wrong.screen: both walks are run on the same row of cards with both points left standing where they were dropped, one counted from the left and one from the right, and each answer is read back with its places counted outward from its own point. The leading digit of the child's answer is lit in the ones column, where it is standing for whole ones, and the two answers stay on the stage together.

wrong.why: several answers in a row with one digit in front of the point make a shape that is easy to copy, and copying a shape is faster than counting.
wrong.move: drops the point after the first digit every time, because the first few answers happened to come out looking like that.
wrong.screen: the counter is read out again and the point card is sent back to the right hand end and walked in with each step numbered above the card it passes, and it will not drop until the count is met. The child's point stays drawn where it was put, a second row of cards is laid underneath with the counted point in it, and both rows are read back from their own points outwards.

phases.screen: the numerator laid out in digit cards with the point card at its right hand end
phases.soWhat: The point goes in from the right hand end of the numerator, one digit for each zero underneath.
phases.concept: Placing the point from the right

phases.win: the zeros settle in front of the digits and every place is filled from the point outwards
phases.does: takes zeros from the tray and fills the empty places on the left
phases.goal: the filling zeros go on the left of the digits, between them and the point
phases.says: The digits have run out. Which side are the empty places on?
phases.check: Turn three over a hundred into a decimal. Where did the filling zero go, and which side of the digits is that?
phases.feels: the gap is always on the side nearest the point, so that is the side the zeros go in on
phases.hands: Hand each group a fraction whose numerator is shorter than the zeros underneath call for, with loose digit cards and loose zero cards. Lay the digits from the right hand end, then look at where the gap is. Say the direction out loud together and make the class say it back: the filling zeros go on the LEFT of the digits, between them and the point, because the places still empty are the ones nearest the point.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many places are still empty? Second rung, the phase's: which side of the digits are they on? Third rung: the row is cut to one digit card over a hundred and the child fills the one empty place. The grey zero key stays open.

wrong.why: the printed rule on the page sends the zeros to the right of the numerator. That is the wrong side and it is never what the worked example printed under it does: that example places a zero before the nine, two zeros before the four and a zero before the sixty-five, and says the word before all three times.
wrong.move: hangs the filling zeros on the right hand end of the digits, so nine hundredths is built out of nine hundred.
wrong.screen: the child's zeros stay hanging exactly where they were hung and the row is read out as the number it now is, which is nine hundred rather than nine. The empty places are then lit again between the point and the digits, on their left, with the short arrow drawn running inward from the point, and a second row is laid underneath with the grey zeros walked into those places instead. Both rows stay standing.

wrong.why: the digits that were given have all been used and the row looks finished, and a place with nothing in it does not look like a place at all.
wrong.move: lays the short numerator down and drops the point without filling anything, so three over a hundred comes out as three tenths.
wrong.screen: the counter is read out again against the row, and the empty place nearest the point is drawn and held lit with the arrow running inward to it, so that the number of places the answer actually has can be counted off against the number the counter is holding. The child's answer stays written, a grey zero is offered from the tray, and both answers are read back with their places counted outward from the point.

phases.screen: a short numerator with places still empty between it and the point
phases.soWhat: A filling zero goes on the left of the digits, between them and the point, and never on their right hand end.
phases.concept: When the numerator is too short

phases.win: both answers stand together and the distance bar says how many times out the wrong one is
phases.does: runs the wrong side lane to its answer and measures the gap between the two
phases.goal: zeros on the wrong side make the number bigger instead of smaller
phases.says: Try it the other way and see where it lands. How far apart are they?
phases.check: A child turns four over a thousand into a decimal by hanging the zeros on the right hand end instead of on the left, in front of the four. How far out is the answer?
phases.feels: the wrong side does not look wrong, it looks finished, and that is exactly what makes it worth measuring
phases.hands: Run the wrong side once, in public, all the way to its answer, so that it is never a mystery afterwards. Write nine hundredths properly on one line and then, underneath, hang the zeros on the right of the nine and carry that working through to its end. Put the two answers side by side and ask how far apart they are. Then do the same with four over a thousand and let the class say which of the two mistakes cost more.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what did the second lane come out with? Second rung, the phase's: is that bigger or smaller than the fraction asked for? Third rung: both lanes are cut to a single digit numerator over a hundred and the child runs them side by side. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: every step of that lane really was carried out properly, and a tidy answer at the end of careful work is hard to doubt.
wrong.move: takes the second lane's answer as the right one, because it came out a tidy whole number and the working was done carefully.
wrong.screen: both answers are carried down to the grid and the strip and drawn at their real sizes, one as a few cells of a hundred and the other as nine whole ones laid out along the stage, so the two are seen rather than compared on the line. The distance bar writes how many times apart they are, both answers stay standing where they were made, and nothing is marked on either of them.

wrong.why: two workings that each ran without a hitch look like two ways of doing one job, and the chapter has already shown a fraction and a decimal being two ways of writing one amount.
wrong.move: decides both answers must be right in their own way, since each lane followed a rule it was given.
wrong.screen: the question the fraction asked is read out again at the top of the stage and both answers are held against it in turn, each one turned back into a fraction on the bench and stood beside the fraction it started from. One comes back to it and one does not, and the one that does not is left standing beside what it actually came to, with the distance bar still drawn between the two answers.

phases.screen: the same fraction loaded into both lanes with the distance bar still empty
phases.soWhat: Zeros on the left make a number smaller and zeros on the right make it bigger, and this step wants smaller.
phases.concept: Why the side matters so much

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when the second lane is let go. The same fraction runs down both lanes at once and in step: above, the zeros walk into the empty places on the left of the digits and the point card comes in from the right hand end; below, the zeros hang themselves past the right hand end and that lane's point card comes in from the right of what they built. Both lanes reach a finished answer on the same tick and neither is marked. The distance bar then draws itself between the two answers and writes how many times apart they are, and the two sit there side by side for as long as anybody wants to look at them, with the voice saying nothing about either of them.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a fraction stands at the top with its denominator lit and the zero counter beside it empty. On the second the numerator lies out in digit cards with the point card waiting just past their right hand end and the counter already set. On the third a short numerator lies out with the counter set higher than the cards can reach, so the places still empty are drawn and lit between the point and the digits, and the zero tray stands open beneath them. On the fourth the same fraction is loaded into both lanes, the upper one worked and the lower one untouched, with the distance bar drawn empty between them. The running count at the top left holds the fractions turned against the fractions this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the lit denominator, or the point card at the right hand end, or the empty place nearest the point, or the untouched lower lane, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how many zeros are underneath. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any numerator over ten, a hundred or a thousand, with the zero tray, the wrong side lane and the distance bar all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on counting the zeros underneath, walking the point in from the right, filling the empty places on the left, and what the wrong side costs.
voiceLines: Count the zeros underneath first. That is how many places you are going to need.
Count the zeros underneath. That is how many places you need.
Start at the right hand end and walk the point in. Count as you go.
The digits have run out. Which side are the empty places on?
Try it the other way and see where it lands. How far apart are they?
Another fraction. Count what is underneath before you touch anything above it.
Free play. Any numerator, any of the three denominators, wrong side lane and distance bar open.
Send the point card back to the right hand end and walk it in again, counting.
Every point walked in from the right, and every filling zero standing in front of the digits.

observations.why: Each zero underneath is one more split by ten, and each split by ten is one more decimal place.
observations.soWhat: The number of decimal places comes from counting zeros, so a hundred asks for two places and not for three.
observations.observe: The counter read the zeros of the denominator, not its digits, and never showed anything else.

observations.why: The last digit of the numerator is the one that has to land in the last decimal place the denominator calls for.
observations.soWhat: The point is counted in from the right, and counting in from the left lands a digit in the ones place instead.
observations.observe: The point card always started at the right hand end of the digits and walked leftwards.

observations.why: The digits were laid from the right hand end, so the gap they left is on their left, between them and the point.
observations.soWhat: A filling zero goes in front of the digits, on the left, and never on their right hand end.
observations.observe: When the digits ran out, the places left empty were the ones nearest the point.

observations.why: Zeros hung on the right hand end make a number bigger, and the working that follows them is carried out perfectly correctly.
observations.soWhat: A neat answer arrived at from the wrong side is still the wrong answer, which is why the side is worth saying out loud.
observations.observe: The second lane reached a tidy answer that was a hundred times too big, and nothing about it looked wrong.

description: Count the zeros underneath, walk the point in from the right, and fill the empty places on the left when the digits run out.

writing the weight of the turmeric powder in decimal

source_tool.description: A fraction stands at the top of the stage with its denominator lit, and a zero counter beside it turns the zeros underneath into a number of decimal places. The numerator is laid out below as separate digit cards in a row, with a point card waiting just past their right hand end. The point card slides leftwards one digit at a time and the counter tracks every step, so the point cannot be dropped until it has moved as many digits as there are zeros below. Where the digits run out before the count is met, the places still empty are drawn and lit between the point and the digits already there, that is on their LEFT, and a zero tray offers zeros to fill them. A zero dropped past the right hand end is refused and springs back, the empty places on the left are lit again, and a short arrow is redrawn running inward from the point to the place that is waiting. A second lane below runs the same fraction with the zeros hung past the right hand end instead and carries it all the way to its answer, and a distance bar is then drawn between the two answers with the size of the gap written along it. Neither lane is marked. The two answers simply stand together and the bar measures them.
source_tool.art_direction: Digit cards and a sliding point card / Picture book

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a strip that can be cut, a ten by ten grid whose cells can be tapped, digit cards that can be picked up, a point card of its own, a ruled place chart with a heading over every column, a kitchen scale with a printing display, and a balance beam.

A whole is always drawn split into parts of the same size, with the parts touching so that the whole is still one thing. Exactly the stated number of parts is drawn, exactly the stated number of them is shaded, and no part overlaps another.

A decimal is always drawn with its point standing clearly between the two parts and never floating above or below the line. Where the two parts are named, the whole number part is named on the left and the decimal part on the right.

A place chart always carries a named heading over every column, holds one digit to a column, and keeps a column of its own for the dot between the ones and the tenths. A bare row of digits with no chart behind it is never used to teach place value.

A zero filling an empty decimal place is drawn arriving from the point outwards, on the left of the digits already there, with a short arrow running inward from the point. That arrow never runs the other way.

A zero printed on the end of a decimal is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit, and it is never dimmed, shrunk, tidied away or quietly dropped. The whole teaching of the closing topic is that it counts.

Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one above the other, with whatever measures the difference between them drawn in between. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
A column, a place or a part is told apart by its label first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a part or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. A digit to the left of the point is deep blue and a digit to the right of it is green, with the decimal point itself vermilion between them in every tool without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is one dot cannot afford a frame where the dot has to be hunted for. A part standing for tenths is amber, one standing for hundredths is rose and one standing for thousandths is sky blue, and those three hold from the strip to the grid to the chart. A zero holding a place open is grey, whether it was filled in on the left of a short numerator or printed on the end of a measurement, because it is the one digit here doing a job rather than counting something. Grey never means faint: such a zero is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. All of that holds in greyscale, because a filling zero is told apart by the short arrow running inward from the point, and a printed zero on the end by the place counter that lights it.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Send the point card back to the right hand end and walk it in again, counting.
voice.onNext: Another fraction. Count what is underneath before you touch anything above it.
voice.opening: Count the zeros underneath first. That is how many places you are going to need.
voice.onFinish: Every point walked in from the right, and every filling zero standing in front of the digits.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any numerator, any of the three denominators, wrong side lane and distance bar open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Placing the point from the right
When the numerator is too short
Why the side matters so much

placement.where: After the zeros in the denominator have been counted aloud, and before the first short numerator is met. The tool is what runs the wrong side all the way to its answer and stands it beside the right one, which a written page can only do by printing a mistake and leaving it there.

answer_key.rule: Count the zeros in the denominator. That is how many decimal places the answer has. Then slide the point into the numerator that many digits in from its right hand end. If the numerator has fewer digits than that, the places still empty are the ones nearest the point, so the filling zeros go on the LEFT of the digits already there, between them and the point. A zero put there is a padding zero, and it always goes in front of the digits and never on the right hand end. Nine hundredths needs two places and nine supplies one, so one zero goes in front of the nine and the answer is 0.09. Four thousandths needs three, so two zeros go in front of the four. Sixty-five thousandths needs three and has two, so one zero goes in front of the sixty-five and the answer is 0.065. Zeros hung on the right hand end instead make the number bigger, which is the opposite of what this step is for.
answer_key.wrong: The zero counter is read out again, the point card is slid back to the right hand end and walked in one digit at a time, and the places still empty are lit on the left of the digits before the zero tray is offered. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The denominator is a hundred, and a hundred is written with two zeros.
Two zeros underneath means two decimal places in the answer, one for each zero.
The numerator 356 already has three digits, so the point goes two digits in from its right hand end, giving 3.56.
items.answer: Two decimal places, because the hundred underneath has two zeros, and the decimal is 3.56
items.question: How many decimal places does 356/100 need, and how do you know? Write the decimal as well.
items.checkpoint: The zeros in the denominator count the decimal places, one place for each zero.
items.misconception: Counting the digits in the denominator instead of its zeros, and asking for three places.

steps: A thousand underneath has three zeros, so three decimal places are needed.
The numerator 617 has exactly three digits, so the point slides three digits in from its right hand end and lands in front of the six.
A zero is written in the ones place to hold it open, giving 0.617.
items.question: Write 617/1000 as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: The point is counted in from the right hand end of the numerator, never from the left.
items.misconception: Counting in from the left instead, and writing 6.17, which puts the six in the ones place where it is worth a whole one.

steps: A hundred underneath has two zeros, so two decimal places are needed.
The numerator is 3, which is one digit, so one place is still empty once the three has been laid down.
The empty place is the one nearest the point, so the zero goes in front of the three, giving 0.03.
items.answer: 0.03, with the zero placed in front of the three
items.question: Write 3/100 as a decimal, and say where the filling zero goes.
items.checkpoint: A filling zero goes on the left of the digits, between them and the point.
items.misconception: Hanging the zero on the right of the three and writing 0.30, which is ten times too big.

steps: Hanging three zeros on the right hand end of the six builds 6000, and counting three digits in from the right of that gives 6.000, which is just 6.
Six thousandths is a tiny amount, so an answer of six whole ones cannot possibly be right.
The zeros belong in front of the six, filling the two places nearest the point, which gives 0.006.
items.answer: They get 6, which is a thousand times too big. The answer is 0.006
items.question: A child turns 6/1000 into a decimal by hanging three zeros on the right hand end of the six and then counting three digits in from the right. What do they get, and what should it be?
items.checkpoint: Zeros on the left make a number smaller and zeros on the right make it bigger, and this step wants smaller.
items.misconception: Following the rule as it is written rather than as the worked example below it does it.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How many decimal places does a denominator of a thousand call for?
items.final_answer: Three, one for each zero in the thousand

items.question: How many zeros are in the denominator of 29/10, and how many digits go after the point?
items.final_answer: One zero, so one digit goes after the point

items.question: Write 5/100 as a decimal, and say which side the filling zero goes on.
items.final_answer: 0.05, and the zero goes on the left, in front of the five

items.question: A child writes 4/100 as 4.00 by hanging the zeros on the right hand end of the four. How far out is that, and what is the right answer?
items.final_answer: It is a hundred times too big. The right answer is 0.04, with one zero placed in front of the four

items.question: Turmeric powder is sold as 5/10 of a kilogram. Write that weight as a decimal, and say why no zero has to go in front of the five.
items.final_answer: 0.5 kg, because only one decimal place is wanted and the five fills it on its own

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: counts the zeros in the denominator and sets how many decimal places are needed
lays the numerator out one digit to a card
slides in from the right hand end, one digit at a time
lights the places still waiting, on the left of the digits, between them and the point
hands over zeros for the empty places and refuses a drop past the right hand end
runs the same fraction with the zeros hung on the right, all the way to its answer
draws the gap between the two answers and writes how many times out the wrong one is
says the finished decimal with its places counted outward from the point

teaching_notes: Say the direction out loud every single time, and make the class say it back. The filling zeros go on the LEFT of the digits, between them and the point, because the places still empty are the ones nearest the point. The printed rule for this step sends them the other way, and the worked example directly beneath it does the opposite and says the word before three separate times: a zero placed in front of the nine to give 0.09, two zeros in front of the four to give 0.004, and a zero in front of the sixty-five to give 0.065. Teach the example, not the sentence above it. Then run the wrong side once, in public, all the way to its answer, so that it is never a mystery. Nine hundredths with the zeros hung on the right builds nine hundred, and the point counted in from there lands on nine whole ones, which is a hundred times what was wanted and looks completely tidy written down. That is what the second lane is for: the two answers stand together and the gap between them can be measured rather than asserted. Every answer printed in this chapter is arithmetically right, so nothing that checks the sums would ever have caught this one. Keep the zero counter locked on until the counting is automatic, and read every finished decimal back with its places counted from the point, because that is the same count run in reverse and it catches a slipped point in seconds.
generation_prompt: Build a converting tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A fraction stands at the top of the working area with its denominator lit and a zero counter beside it that turns the zeros underneath into a number of decimal places. The numerator is laid out below as separate digit cards in a row, with a point card waiting just past their right hand end. The point card slides leftwards one digit at a time, the counter tracking each step, and it cannot be dropped until it has moved as many digits as there are zeros in the denominator. Where the digits run out before the count is met, the places still empty are drawn and lit between the point and the digits already there, that is on their LEFT, and a zero tray offers zeros to fill them. A zero dropped past the right hand end of the digits is refused and springs back, the empty places on the left are lit again, and a short arrow is redrawn running inward from the point to the place that is waiting; nothing is marked. A second lane below runs the same fraction with the zeros hung past the right hand end instead and carries it all the way to its answer, and a distance bar is then drawn between the two answers with the size of the gap written along it. Neither lane is cleared and neither is marked. A read it back control says the finished decimal with its places counted outward from the point. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Count the zeros in the bottom number. Start the point at the right hand end. Walk it in one digit for each zero. If the digits run out, fill the empty places on the left. Never hang a zero on the right hand end.
